issues.description: Constructor 'SealSaloon': The problem statement (UML and text) requires a constructor SealSaloon(String) and states "The constructor takes the saloon name as a String parameter". However, the template usage (Main.java) and the solution implementation (SealSaloon.java) both provide and use a no-argument constructor SealSaloon(). This discrepancy leaves students uncertain whether to implement a constructor that accepts a String and whether to store a saloon name, and may cause compilation/test mismatches depending on which signature is expected by the tests or graders.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the constructor requirement consistent across artifacts. Option A: Update the problem statement and UML to specify a no-argument constructor SealSaloon() and remove the instruction to pass/store a saloon name. Option B (preferred if the name is meaningful): Change the template and solution to provide a public constructor SealSaloon(String name), add a private final String name field with a getter, and update any example usage in Main to pass a name. Ensure the UML, textual description, template code, and solution all use the same constructor signature.

issues.description: Constructor/signature mismatch for SealSaloon: The problem statement specifies a constructor SealSaloon(String) and states the saloon name should be taken as a String parameter and stored for identification. The solution implementation provides only a parameterless constructor public SealSaloon() and does not declare or store any saloon name field (no private final String name or getter). A student reading the problem will expect to implement/use SealSaloon(String) and a name field/getter, but the provided solution API differs, causing an API/identifier mapping inconsistency and potential confusion when implementing or testing.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the implementation match the problem statement: add a public constructor SealSaloon(String name) to SealSaloon.java that stores the provided name in a private final String name field and initialize other attributes (orders, etc.) accordingly; add a public getter getName(). Alternatively, if the no-argument constructor was intentional, update the problem statement to remove the requirement for SealSaloon(String) and the saloon-name field so the specification and implementation agree.
